paper_title: WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Task generalization marks fundamental shift from earlier pretrained NLP models, such as BERT [16], to modern large language models (LLMs) [6, 15, 63]. Whereas earlier models typically require task-specific fine-tuning, single LLM can perform diverse tasks specified through natural-language instructions or few in-context examples, without updating its parameters for each new task. This capability has motivated the pursuit of generalist embodied agents that can translate human instructions into broad repertoire of physical behaviors. Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent an important step toward this goal, transferring knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into robot control [5, 47]. However, understanding an instruction does not automatically provide the physical competence needed to execute it. Bringing task generalization into robotics requires connecting semantic knowledge to the visual dynamics and motor behaviors of physical interaction. 1 Figure 1 Overview of our WorldBridge, foundational WAM for task generalization. WorldBridge utilizes heterogeneous data sources and is trained with simple but effective model architecture in two stages. The bottom panels report task-generalization results under different video and action supervision settings, benchmark performance, and real-world deployment results. Despite substantial progress, prominent focus of embodied generalization research remains robustness to changes in the conditions under which task is performed, including object arrangements, camera viewpoints, lighting, and visual appearance. Benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus systematically evaluate these variations, exposing the brittleness of otherwise successful policies [19]. Task generalization introduces an additional challenge: robot must execute behaviors beyond those covered by its original training tasks. Achieving this capability requires understanding how newly requested task should unfold and producing the actions that realize it, even when corresponding robot demonstrations are scarce or unavailable. World Action Models (WAMs) provide promising foundation for addressing this challenge by coupling visual prediction with action generation. Video offers dense supervision of physical interactions, allowing models to learn how scenes evolve beyond the coverage of action-labeled robot data. DreamZero demonstrates that video priors can support unseen-task execution and transfer from video-only demonstrations [68], while Zero-WAM explores task generalization through in-context human video guidance [75]. Recent advances in native video-action pretraining [72], systematic WAM pretraining [58], and temporal context [24] further strengthen this paradigm. These developments motivate more specific question: how do broader video coverage and additional action supervision contribute to task generalization, and when does the connection between them become the limiting factor? In this work, we investigate task generalization in WAMs through two complementary capabilities: video generalization and action generalization. Video generalization enables model to predict the visual evolution required by tasks beyond its initial training distribution. Action generalization refers to the ability to translate those visual predictions into executable actions beyond the tasks that supplied action supervision. This translation forms video-to-action bridge, serving the role of an inverse dynamics model (IDM). model may predict an appropriate visual future yet lack the action grounding needed to realize it. Conversely, transferable bridge can allow knowledge acquired from additional videos to improve task execution without corresponding action labels, which motivates studying the availability of video and action supervision separately. 2 Figure 2 Task generalization under progressively expanded supervision. Compared with in-domain (ID) video-action training alone (25.07% OOD success rate), adding out-of-distribution (OOD) videos increases success to 55.90%, while adding few paired OOD video-action examples further improves it to 70.70%. Figure 2 illustrates this progression, which we examine by varying supervision for tasks outside an initial in-distribution (ID) training set. With only ID video-action pairs, the model achieves nontrivial but limited generalization, obtaining 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. Adding videos of those OOD tasks while keeping action supervision restricted to the ID set increases OOD success to 55.90%. This improvement suggests that expanded video coverage can support new task execution through bridge learned from ID action supervision. Keeping the video set fixed, adding only one action-labeled demonstration per OOD task further raises success to 70.70%. These rapid gains are consistent with sparse paired examples strengthening the bridge for visual transitions that are already covered by the video data. Together, these observations support complementary account of task generalization: video supervision expands the range of task evolutions WAM can model, while action supervision improves its ability to turn that knowledge into reliable control. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, WAM that couples video prediction and action generation through Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture [35]. WorldBridge maintains separate video and action experts trained with joint flow-matching objective. structured attention mask establishes directional information path from observed context to future video representations and then to action predictions, making predicted visual dynamics an explicit source of conditioning for control. Short-term and long-term visual memories provide information about local motion and task progression. We additionally employ action forcing, assigning independent noise levels to actions within chunk during training so that the action expert learns to predict actions using temporal context at varying levels of corruption. To support learning across heterogeneous sources, we develop unified pretraining data pipeline for robot trajectories and egocentric human demonstrations. The pipeline standardizes control semantics and maps available robot controls and human hand-derived targets into shared 46-dimensional action representation. Dimension-wise validity masks preserve partial supervision across embodiments with different control interfaces. Robot trajectories undergo kinematic and temporal consistency checks, while egocentric hand trajectories are standardized in common reference frame and filtered using geometric and motion constraints. This processing supports broader visual coverage together with usable action supervision, providing common interface for learning the video-to-action bridge across diverse data sources. Our evaluations demonstrate strong performance across range of manipulation tasks. WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on multiple benchmarks, with average success rates of 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0, 80.9% in the RoboTwin 2.0 C2R setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. On RMBench, it matches the best result in our comparison, with an 83.0% success rate. We further conduct real-world evaluations on the Agibot-G2 and AC-1 platforms, covering long-horizon execution, memory-dependent tasks, spatial localization, and bimanual coordination. Together 3 Figure 3 Overview of the WorldBridge model architecture. with our task-generalization study, these results support the value of jointly developing video prediction and action grounding. Our contributions are threefold: We study task generalization in WAMs through the complementary roles of video generalization and action generalization, quantifying the gains from additional task videos and sparse action supervision. We introduce WorldBridge and unified data processing pipeline that connect visual dynamics to executable control across heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations. We evaluate WorldBridge across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, RMBench, DOMINO Level-1, SimplerEnv-WidowX, and RoboDojo, covering diverse manipulation demands and distribution shifts. We further deploy it on AgiBot G2 and ARX AC-1, fine-tuning the same jointly pretrained checkpoint for each platform and evaluating long-horizon execution, memory-dependent interaction, spatial alignment, and bimanual coordination.

sections.title: 2.1.3 Action Forcing
sections.content: When single flow timestep is shared across an entire action chunk, all action tokens are corrupted to the same noise level. Action forcing instead exposes the action expert to chunks containing actions at different noise levels. Since action-token inputs can vary substantially in their noise levels and are difficult to model in isolation, this design encourages each token to rely more on contextual visual information. Specifically, we extend the scalar action flow timestep τa to vector τ = [τa,0, . . . , τa,H1]. For group size g, we independently sample flow timestep sa,k for each group = 0, . . . , H/g 1 from the training flow-matching schedule, independently of the video timestep τv. The timestep assigned to action is For the j-th action in the chunk, the noisy input is τa,j = sa,j/g, = 0, . . . , 1. (cid:101)at+j = (1 τa,j)at+j + τa,jϵa,j, = 0, . . . , 1, (10) (11) where the noise vectors ϵa,j (0, I) are sampled independently, even when actions share flow timestep. Here, actions are represented in the normalized unified action space. Each action is encoded as one token and receives its corresponding flow-time embedding. The action expert therefore processes mixture of relatively clean and highly corrupted actions within the same chunk. Through attention within the action branch, each prediction can use the other actions at their respective noise levels, while also conditioning on future video features. The prediction target remains the flow-matching velocity: a,j = ϵa,j at+j. (12) At inference, all action tokens are initialized with independent standard Gaussian noise and denoised jointly using shared action flow timestep. Thus, varying noise levels across actions or groups are only used during training, while the complete action chunk is generated through joint denoising at inference. 2.1.4 Attention Mask We adopt stage-specific attention masks to control information exchange between video and action tokens within each MoT block. As illustrated in Figure 4, the joint sequence comprises four groups: memory tokens, current frame tokens, future frame tokens, and action tokens. We use densely connected video mask during pretraining and introduce more structured dependencies during post-training. We use stage-specific attention masks to balance flexible multimodal learning during pretraining with an explicit video-to-action pathway during post-training. During pretraining, video tokens attend to all video tokens but not to action tokens, preserving actionindependent video generation. Action tokens attend to both video and action tokens, allowing the action 6 Figure 4 Attention mask design. (a) Attention mask for pretraining. (b) Attention mask for post-training. expert to learn from the full visual and action context. During post-training, memory and current-frame tokens attend to one another; future-video tokens attend to the current-frame and future-video tokens, and action tokens attend to future-video and action tokens. This structure routes information from memory and current observations through predicted future features to action predictions, encouraging actions to be grounded in the modeled visual evolution. For tasks with strong memory demands, we use the pretraining mask instead, allowing action tokens to access memory tokens directly.

sections.title: 2.2.1 Robot Data Processing
sections.content: We curate heterogeneous robot demonstrations through unified pipeline comprising semantic auditing, representation standardization, and trajectory filtering. We first map source-specific state and action fields into shared representation with explicit validity masks. We then trim stationary episode boundaries, remove short trajectories, and apply kinematic and temporal consistency checks. Processing rules are configured for each source and embodiment to accommodate differences in annotation availability, control semantics, and signal characteristics. Semantic Auditing and Representation Standardization. We first check what each source field represents, including joint order, EEF coordinates and rotations, gripper opening direction, and the meaning of recorded actions. State and action are mapped separately because measured state and control target are not interchangeable. Available values are placed in the shared 46-dimensional layout described in Section 2.3.2. Separate state and action masks identify which entries are available; missing or non-finite values are set to zero and masked out. EEF rotations are converted to unit quaternions in (x, y, z, w) order. Gripper values are calibrated for each source so that 0 means fully closed and 1 means fully open. Each dexterous hand has six slots: bending of the little, ring, middle, index, and thumb fingers, followed by thumb rotation. Depending on the robot, we reorder the original channels, combine coupled finger joints, or map shared hand-closure signal to the corresponding finger-bending slots. These slots therefore do not always represent independently measured finger joints. Unsupported hand motions remain masked. Four additional slots store supported waist and torso signals, such as waist pitch and torso lift, with mapping specified for each robot; unused slots remain masked. EEF positions retain their original coordinate frames and units. Relative action targets and training normalization are defined separately in Section 2.3.2. Static Boundary Trimming and Length Filtering. We detect motion from adjacent state differences over dimensions that are valid and finite at both timesteps. transition is considered active if any comparable dimension changes by more than 104 in the stored feature space. We retain the interval spanning the first and last active transitions, including their endpoint frames. This removes stationary prefixes and suffixes while preserving pauses within task execution. Fully stationary episodes with observable states are discarded, whereas episodes without comparable valid state dimensions are left unchanged by this check. We subsequently remove trajectories shorter than 48 frames and update episode and video-window metadata to reflect the retained intervals. Kinematic Consistency Filtering. For sources with comparable joint and EEF annotations, we compute the EEF pose from recorded joint positions using forward kinematics (FK). We account for source-specific base frames and tool definitions before comparing the FK pose with the recorded pose. Let (pFK, RFK) and (pdata, Rdata) denote these two poses at the same timestep. We measure their position and orientation errors as epos = pFK pdata2, erot = arccos (cid:18) tr(R FKRdata) 1 (cid:19) 2 . (13) The argument of arccos is clipped to [1, 1] for numerical stability. frame passes when the applicable errors are below embodiment-specific thresholds, and an episode is retained when sufficient fraction of evaluated frames passes. Invalid required poses count as failures, while position-only configurations omit the orientation 7 Figure 5 Overview of the WorldBridge data processing pipeline. check. For selected sources with an unknown fixed frame relationship, we estimate single rigid transformation per episode before computing the errors. This alignment is used only for consistency assessment. Signal Anomaly and StateAction Consistency Filtering. We apply three complementary signal checks and reject episodes that fail an applicable criterion. Sudden-change detection. We estimate smooth trajectory using median and SavitzkyGolay filtering, then evaluate the residual together with secondand third-order temporal differences. sample is flagged when an excessive residual coincides with an excessive higher-order difference. Robust, channel-specific thresholds distinguish abrupt anomalies from ordinary motion. Quaternion signs are aligned temporarily during detection to avoid artificial discontinuities between equivalent rotations. The smoothing and sign alignment are used for detection and do not replace the stored signals. Stateaction consistency. For comparable joint dimensions with sufficient motion, we compare the directions of changes in smoothed state and action signals. We search offsets within 15 frames and retain the best directional agreement for each eligible dimension. Episodes are rejected when the minimum agreement across eligible dimensions falls below the source-specific threshold. This procedure assesses temporal consistency without shifting the saved action sequences. Extreme-value detection. We estimate the 1st and 99th percentiles from valid samples within each repository. The admissible interval extends beyond these quantiles by the larger of five times their span and channelspecific minimum margin. Episodes containing out-of-range or non-finite active values are rejected. Quaternion, gripper, and dexterous-hand channels are exempt from this range test. Source-specific configurations determine the applicable checks and exemptions. 2.2.2 Ego Data Processing We process egocentric demonstrations into synchronized visual observations and hand-derived action targets. Each sequence contains egocentric RGB frames, camera-to-world poses, and 21 three-dimensional keypoints per hand in consistent MANO ordering. Available task and subtask annotations provide the language context. Our pipeline standardizes the coordinate representation, maps hand geometry into the shared action layout, and filters unreliable supervision using geometric and temporal consistency checks. Coordinate Standardization. To account for the moving egocentric camera, we express future hand geometry in the camera frame of the current observation. Let Tw SE(3) denote the camera-to-world transformation ct at timestep t, and let xct+k be the homogeneous coordinate of hand keypoint observed at future timestep. t+k,j Its coordinate in the current camera frame is t+k,j = (cid:0)Tw xct ct (cid:1)1 Tw ct+k xct+k t+k,j. (14) The reference frame remains fixed throughout the prediction chunk, placing future hand trajectories in common coordinate system despite changes in camera pose. Video and geometry are sampled on shared physical-time schedule to preserve their temporal correspondence. Hand-to-Action Mapping. We derive canonical wrist pose from each transformed hand. The wrist keypoint defines its position, while the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints define its orientation. Specifically, the forward axis points from the wrist toward the centroid of the four finger bases, and least-squares palm plane provides the palm normal. handedness correction gives the left and right hands consistent axis semantics. We additionally extract continuous gripper-openness target from the distance between the thumb tip and virtual opposing finger formed from the index and middle fingertips. Normalizing this distance by palm width reduces dependence on hand size. For dexterous-hand supervision, finger bending and thumb opposition are mapped to six bounded joint-position targets per hand. Quality Filtering and Validity Masks. We assess hand annotations using biomechanical plausibility, coordinate bounds, bone lengths, and temporal motion statistics, including velocity, acceleration, and jerk. Motion derivatives are computed using actual timestamps and world-coordinate hand trajectories. Camera rotations are checked for orthogonality and determinant consistency. Dataset-specific thresholds accommodate differences in motion statistics across sources. Quality annotations are consumed at the sampled action timesteps. Targets associated with rejected frames are masked, while windows with more than 20% rejected action timesteps are discarded. An invalid reference camera pose invalidates the corresponding action chunk. During action construction, non-finite coordinates, padded frames, and degenerate hand geometry are further excluded through validity masks. Missing observations of one hand do not automatically invalidate the other. This preserves usable visual context and partial hand supervision without treating unavailable action dimensions as valid zero-valued targets.

We jointly optimize the video and action experts with equally weighted video and action flow-matching losses, using AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at norm of 0.5. Both experts use base learning rate of 104. We pretrain for 60,000 optimizer steps, linearly increasing the learning rate from 1010 to 9.9 105 during the first 2,000 steps. Training uses BF16 on 64 GPUs, with 12 samples per GPU and two gradient-accumulation steps, giving an effective batch size of 12 64 2 = 1, 536. Sampling and Training Windows. We sample robot and ego data with probabilities 0.7 and 0.3, respectively, and weight repositories within each source category by usable physical duration. Each chunk contains = 32 action targets and eight future video frames, with one video frame per four action timesteps. Robot and ego action grids are sampled at 15 Hz and 30 Hz, respectively. For sources configured with three camera views, we spatially compose synchronized main-camera and left/right wrist-camera images into single frame at each timestep. The main view occupies the top region, while the two wrist views, each resized to half the main views width and height, are placed side by side below it, forming T-shaped layout. The composite frame is then bilinearly resized to 320 384 pixels (width height) without added padding and encoded as one video stream by the shared video VAE. Sources configured for single view use the selected camera image resized to the same resolution. The same camera layout is applied to memory, current, and future frames. The current absolute action record is encoded as 46-dimensional state token; action targets use the normalized unified representation. 11 Attention Mask and Noise Sampling. We use the pretraining mask in Fig. 4 (a). Video tokens attend to all video tokens and do not attend to the action branch. Action-branch tokens attend to all video tokens and to one another. Thus, video prediction is independent of action inputs, while action prediction can use the full video context. The video and action flow timesteps are sampled independently. Action forcing is disabled in this pretraining configuration: all actions within chunk share one action flow timestep. Memory Configuration. Both short-term and long-term visual memory are enabled, with four observations at each scale. On the source-specific action time grid, short-term observations have offsets [8, 6, 4, 2], while long-term observations have offsets [128, 96, 64, 32] relative to the current observation. Thus, δs = 2 and δl = = 32 in Section 2.1.2. The causal video VAE compresses these histories into two memory latent frames alongside the current-frame latent. All three provide clean conditioning context, with flow timestep zero, under the pretraining attention mask.

sections.title:
2.4 Efficiency Implementation
Inference acceleration. We accelerate inference by decoupling video and action denoising. At deployment,
a naive implementation performs N denoising steps in both the video and action branches, typically with
N = 10. Multi-step denoising in the computationally intensive video branch substantially increases inference
cost. For acceleration, we perform n synchronized denoising steps that update both branches and construct
per-layer video key–value features; the remaining N − n action denoising steps reuse the features from the
final synchronized step. The directional attention mask permits this reuse without feedback from action
tokens to video tokens, although freezing early video features approximates joint denoising. Visual features
are refreshed for every observation, and future-video RGB decoding is omitted. Action chunks, comprising 48
steps in the paper setting, amortize observation encoding across the predicted sequence.
sections.content: We further accelerate action inference through operator fusion and CUDA Graph replay. The action denoising computation is compiled with torch.compile into optimized GPU kernels, fusing compatible operations to reduce intermediate memory traffic and kernel launches. CUDA Graphs capture the resulting GPU execution sequence and replay it during subsequent denoising steps, reducing Python dispatch and CPU-side kernel-launch overhead. The policy runs in BF16 under inference mode. We also reuse language context, scheduler metadata, and timestep-dependent AdaLN tensors, and evaluate QKV projection, KV-buffer, and fixed-shape attention optimizations. Compilation and graph capture are completed during warmup. Asynchronous execution. To maintain smooth robot motion despite model inference latency, we decouple policy inference from action execution in real-world experiments. The server computes the next action chunk on the GPU while the client continues executing the current chunk. The client prefetches new predictions based on the remaining execution time of its current plan, with at most one outstanding request to avoid accumulating stale observations. Each predicted chunk is timestamped relative to its input observation. Upon receipt, expired actions are discarded, while the remaining actions retain their original execution times. The client resamples the chunk once onto the 100 Hz servo grid, and the C++ controller handles trajectory splicing and final amplitude limiting.

Once this action grounding is established, additional videos can further improve OOD task execution, whereas increasing action supervision offers limited additional gains in this regime.

From top to bottom: arranging flowers, scanning drinks, separating LEGO bricks, packing books, sorting screws, and hanging cups. Arrows and circles highlight key operations, including sequential flower insertion, bimanual brick separation, and precise placement. The drink-scanning task probes three aspects of memory: remembering post-scan placement destinations, tracking previously scanned drinks, and processing the newly introduced drink last. grasp selection with alignment of the handle and hook. On AC-1, separating LEGO bricks requires repeated bimanual disassembly of connected bricks followed by sorting into bins by color. It tests long-horizon coordination, stable grasping during separation, and classification-guided placement as the assembly changes throughout execution. Sorting screws requires grasping small screws and nuts, placing them into their designated compartments, and closing the box. It combines fine-grained object discrimination with precise grasping and placement, requiring correct part selection and accurate manipulation within single sequence. Packing books requires opening schoolbag, inserting book while maintaining access to the opening, and final closing the bag. It tests long-horizon manipulation of deformable container: the robot must coordinate bag opening with subsequent insertion despite changes in the bags shape and accessible geometry. We compare WorldBridge with π0.5 [47], Motus [3], FastWAM [70], and LingBot-VA [33], and evaluate WorldBridge variant without our joint videoaction pretraining. All methods are fine-tuned on the same demonstration set for each task and evaluated over 20 trials with varied initial object positions or orientations. Success requires completing the entire task without human assistance to the robot; introducing drink during scanning is prescribed interaction. We report per-task and average success rates across all tasks. Figure 7 Task success rates across five methods. Overall real-robot performance. Figure 7 summarizes the quantitative results. WorldBridge achieves an average success rate of 72.5%, compared with 57.5% for π0.5, 39.2% for LingBot-VA, 29.2% for FastWAM, and 10.8% for Motus. It achieves the highest success rate on five tasks and ties π0.5 at 80% on separating LEGO bricks. On G2, WorldBridge reaches 70% on arranging flowers and 85% on hanging cups, compared with 65% and 75% for π0.5, respectively. These results cover both extended manipulation sequences and precise spatial placement; the larger gap on scanning drinks is discussed below. On AC-1, WorldBridge achieves 80% on packing books and 55% on sorting screws, exceeding π0.5 at 75% and 45%, respectively, while matching its LEGO disassembly performance. Sorting screws remains the least successful task for WorldBridge, identifying precise small-part sorting as remaining challenge within this suite. Cross-embodiment experiments. Cross-embodiment adaptation follows our unified 46-dimensional action representation, which maps robot-specific control variables into fixed semantic slots and uses dimension-wise validity masks to exclude unavailable components from pretraining supervision. This common interface allows the action expert to learn from heterogeneous control data while preserving the semantics of the available controls. For the real-robot experiments, we fine-tune the same jointly pretrained checkpoint separately for G2 and AC-1, transferring the shared video and action experts and adapting the state and action interfaces to each platform. G2 uses 16-dimensional native commands comprising seven joints per arm and two grippers, whereas AC-1 uses 14-dimensional commands comprising six joints per arm and two grippers. Platform-specific input and output adapters connect the common pretrained experts to these native interfaces. Benefits of joint videoaction pretraining. The paired WorldBridge results in Fig. 7 show that omitting joint videoaction pretraining reduces average success to 46.7%, an absolute decrease of 25.8 percentage points. This variant retains the pretrained Wan video backbone [56], so the comparison measures the additional benefit of our joint pretraining stage. Pretraining improves all six tasks. The largest gain occurs on sorting screws, where success increases from 10% to 55%; packing books and separating LEGO bricks each improve from 50% to 80%. The screw-sorting sequence in Fig. 6 illustrates the fine grasping and compartment placement required by the task with the largest pretraining gain. On G2, the gains are 15 percentage points for arranging flowers, 20 for hanging cups, and 15 for scanning drinks. The improvements therefore span precise small-object handling, spatial alignment, coordinated manipulation, and memory-dependent execution. In particular, the substantial gains on the AC-1 tasks support the value of joint pretraining for downstream adaptation under the available task demonstrations. In this task, the robot must grasp scanner, scan the original drinks Memory-dependent drink scanning. in order, and finally scan an additional drink introduced by human during execution. Correct execution requires three aspects of memory. First, the robot must remember each drinks placement destination after scanning, preserving the spatial association across grasping, scanning, and placement. sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models use pretrained vision-language models to learn robot policies that follow language instructions. RT-2 transfers web knowledge to robot control [5], and OpenVLA provides an open-source model trained on diverse robot demonstrations [28]. π0 uses flow matching to generate continuous actions [4], while π0.5 uses heterogeneous training data to improve generalization across environments [47]. However, these models still struggle with new tasks when action-labeled demonstrations are limited or unavailable. Combining action prediction with world modeling offers way to learn both how tasks unfold and how to execute them. WorldVLA unifies image and action understanding and generation in an autoregressive model, showing that jointly learning the two can improve both action prediction and visual generation [10]. Video-based World Action Models (WAMs) further use video priors to support robot control beyond the coverage of action-labeled data. DreamZero shows that these priors can support unseen-task execution and transfer from video-only demonstrations [68], while Zero-WAM uses human videos as in-context guidance for new tasks [75]. Other studies explore video-action pretraining [58, 72] and temporal context through longer observation histories or persistent memory [24, 66]. Our work examines how video coverage and action supervision contribute to task generalization, and how the video-to-action bridge turns predicted visual dynamics into executable actions.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented WorldBridge, World Action Model that connects visual dynamics to executable control for task generalization. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video coverage and action grounding: additional task videos enable transfer beyond the tasks providing action supervision, while even single actionlabeled demonstration per new task substantially improves execution. Guided by these findings, WorldBridge couples video and action experts through structured attention and joint flow matching, incorporating temporal memory, action forcing, and unified pre-training on heterogeneous robot and egocentric demonstrations. Experiments across simulation benchmarks and two real-robot platforms demonstrate strong manipulation performance and the benefits of joint videoaction pretraining. These results suggest that advancing task generalization requires both broader visual experience and transferable video-to-action bridge. Extending this bridge to more diverse tasks with less action supervision remains an important direction for future work.
